newsitem.title: USA: tennis-U.S. BANKS ON SELES TO STOP SPANISH ARMADA.
newsitem.headline: tennis-U.S. BANKS ON SELES TO STOP SPANISH ARMADA.

text.p: The United States is banking on a high-performance European import to break Spain's stranglehold on the Fed Cup when the two nations meet in the finals this weekend.

Co-world number one Monica Seles has been tabbed by U.S. captain Billie Jean King to spearhead her adopted country's campaign to claim the trophy the United States last held in 1990 -- not coincidentally the last year Spain missed the finals.
There has been one superpower in Fed Cup competition this decade -- Spain -- featuring the most successful 1-2 punch the women's international team championship has seen since its inception in 1963.

"There are two good reasons why Spain has won everything the last few years," said King, "and that is Arantxa Sanchez Vicario and Conchita Martinez -- the number two and three players in the world. They are the reason that Spain has been so dominating."
Since the pair teamed for Federation Cup in the late 1980s they have been world beaters.

The battling Barcelona baseliners have carried Spain to four Fed Cup titles in the last five years, including the last three. The finals begin with two singles on Saturday, followed by reverse singles and doubles on Sunday.

This weekend's tie on the indoor carpet at the Atlantic City Convention Centre will mark Spain's sixth consecutive appearance in the finals and eighth in nine years -- all based on the play of Sanchez and Martinez, who usually join forces to play doubles as well as contesting the singles.
For the third year in a row Spain and the United States meet at the last stage, with one significant difference this time around -- Seles.

"I wanted to be in the Olympics and Fed Cup for many years," said the Yugoslav-born Seles, who became a U.S. citizen in 1994 but has felt like an all-American girl since she laid eyes on her first Florida shopping mall at age 12.
Seles, now 22, made her Fed Cup debut in July in the semifinals in Japan, where she easily won both her singles, crunching Kimiko Date with the loss of just two games.
Seles faltered in the quarter-finals at the Olympics, but Fed Cup teammates Lindsay Davenport (singles) and Mary Joe Fernandez (doubles) walked away with gold.
And Davenport's golden moment came at the expense of none other than Arantxa Sanchez Vicario.

Linda Wild completes the American quartet, giving King a number of singles and doubles options. Davenport and Fernandez won the French Open doubles title this year and Davenport combined with Wild in the 5-0 semifinal win over Japan.
Sanchez brings an impressive 35-11 Fed Cup singles record into the tie, while Martinez boasts a formidable 36-6 singles mark, 4-0 this year.

It was former Wimbledon champion Martinez who proved the saviour in Spain's 3-2 semifinal win over France, taking both her singles matches when Sanchez faltered, then teaming with Sanchez for the clinching doubles win.

The last time the United States beat Spain in a final was back in 1989 when another rather impressive European import -- Martina Navratilova -- teamed with Chris Evert to beat a much younger, and no doubt awestruck, Sanchez and Martinez.
The Spanish duo may not be in awe of Seles, but neither has figured a way to beat her either.

Seles is 12-1 against Sanchez, including a victory last Sunday in a final in Tokyo. She raised her record to 9-0 versus Martinez with a straight sets semifinal win at the U.S. Open earlier this month.
Still, the Spaniards carry a wealth of Fed Cup finals experience into the weekend.
"She has the pressure," Sanchez said of Seles, who has never played a final in the team format. "(We'll) just go out and see what happens, sometimes statistics are not true."
The Spaniards won't have the home court advantage as they did last year in Valencia. But as always, Sanchez is prepared to battle until the last ball bounces twice.
"We made the court as slow as can be last year because the Americans didn't like it," she recalled.
"This surface is much faster but as a pro you have to know how to play on any surface, and keep fighting."
